title: How to Revitalize a Dying Church
excerpt: Revitalization is not a program you install but a death the pastor must enter before the congregation can live.
body:
The numbers came to me on a Tuesday. Average attendance down a third over four years, the giving following it like a shadow, three funerals and no baptisms, and a roof that would not last another Michigan winter. I had the spreadsheet open on the kitchen table when one of my sons asked what was wrong, and I could not answer him, because the honest answer was that I did not know how to make a dying thing live. That is where every revitalization actually begins. Not with a plan. With a man who has run out of plans.

We reach for the wrong question first. We ask how to grow the church, as if growth were the disease working backward, as if the absence of people were the whole of the sickness. But a church can grow numerically and be dead, and a church can shrink and be more alive than it has been in twenty years. The real question is not how to reverse the decline. The real question is whether the body in front of us still wants to be a church at all, or whether it wants to be a club with a steeple, a place where the familiar faces gather to manage their own slow ending with dignity. You cannot answer that question with a survey. You answer it by preaching the gospel and watching who flinches.

There is a strong case against pastors like me even using the word revitalization, and it deserves to be heard at full strength. The critics say that most revitalization talk is church-growth machinery in vestments, that we have taken the language of the New Testament and welded it to attendance metrics borrowed from retail, and that the result is a generation of pastors who measure the Spirit by the parking lot. They are right about more than we would like. Eugene Peterson spent a career warning that the pastoral vocation had been colonized by the shopkeeper's mentality, that we had become managers of religious consumers, fussing over the displays (Peterson 1993, 1). When the critics say our revitalization is often just a more spiritual word for marketing, they have caught us. So let me answer the strongest version of the charge, not the weak one. The strong version is this. A church is not a business and cannot be saved by business means, because its life was never its own to begin with. That is true. And it is precisely why revitalization is possible. A thing that lives by its own strength dies when that strength runs out. A thing that lives by resurrection has a future its accountants cannot see.

Which is why I keep returning to one text, the one I cannot preach without my voice catching. The prophet is set down in the middle of a valley, and the valley is full of bones, and the bones are very many and they are very dry (Ezekiel 37:2 ESV). This is not a church with a budget problem. This is a graveyard with no expectation of a morning. And the Lord asks Ezekiel the only question that matters in a dying church. Son of man, can these bones live. Notice that God does not ask whether Ezekiel can make them live. He asks whether Ezekiel believes they can. And Ezekiel, who is wiser than every consultant I have ever hired, refuses to lie in either direction. He will not say yes, because the evidence is bone-dry against him. He will not say no, because he has met this God before. O Lord God, you know (Ezekiel 37:3 ESV). That is the posture revitalization requires. Not optimism. Not despair. Surrender of the verdict to the only One who has ever raised anything.

We forget how we got here, and the forgetting keeps us reaching for shallow cures. The decline of the inherited church in the West is not a failure of one denomination or one decade. Lesslie Newbigin came home to England in 1974 after thirty-eight years as a missionary in India and found a country that had become, in his words, a pagan society whose public life was governed by assumptions no longer Christian, and harder to reach than any non-Christian culture he had served abroad (Newbigin 1986, 20). He saw what most pastors still refuse to see. The dying church is not a patient with a treatable infection. It is the visible edge of a civilization that quietly relocated its faith from the church to the self somewhere between the Enlightenment and the shopping mall. Charles Taylor traced the architecture of it, the long migration from a world where belief was effortless to a world where belief is one option among many and not the easiest one (Taylor 2007, 3). If you do not see the size of the problem, you will treat a five-hundred-year shift with a six-week sermon series, and you will fail, and you will blame the people in the pews who are simply the last to feel the cold.

So what do we actually do. Here is the reversal that took me years to accept. The pastor does not revitalize the church. The pastor is the first one who has to die. I came into a struggling congregation convinced my energy was the cure, that if I prayed harder and worked longer and programmed smarter the bones would rattle. What I learned is that my frantic competence was part of the death. I was offering them a healthier version of self-reliance, and a church cannot be saved from self-reliance by a more spiritual self-reliance. The dry bones do not come together because the prophet is impressive. They come together because the prophet speaks a word he did not invent over a situation he cannot fix, and then waits for a wind he cannot summon. Prophesy to the breath, the Lord says, and Ezekiel does, and the breath comes (Ezekiel 37:9 ESV). The pastor's whole authority in revitalization is the authority of a man with nothing in his hands but a borrowed word.

This is where the cross does its work, and it does it on the leader before it does it on the congregation. The law comes first, and the law in a dying church is brutal in its honesty. It says your decline is not merely demographic. It says you have loved your own comfort more than the lost neighbor, that you have made the sanctuary a museum of your own memories, that the empty pews are partly the fruit of doors you were happy to keep shut. I have to preach that to myself before I preach it to anyone, because I have done it. I have protected my own schedule from the very people Christ died to reach. The law leaves us in the valley with the bones, and that is exactly where it is supposed to leave us, because grace cannot raise a church that still believes it is only sleeping. Only when we have agreed with God that we are dead can the next sentence land. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves (Ezekiel 37:13 ESV). Not when you fix your graves. When I open them.

The practical work follows from this and never precedes it. You will need to preach the whole counsel of God again, not management wisdom in a clerical collar. You will need to know the names and the wounds of the people actually in the room, because Newbigin was right that the only hermeneutic of the gospel a watching world will accept is a congregation that believes it (Newbigin 1989, 227). You will need to raise up others rather than hoard the work, to be patient across years rather than quarters, to bury programs that died long ago and stop holding their funerals every Sunday. None of that is the source of the life. All of it is the riverbed the life runs through when it comes.

My congregation is not what it was. Some of that is grace I can point to, baptisms I did not expect, a young family in the third pew who found Christ from outside everything. Some of it is still bone and still dry, and I have made my peace with not knowing the ending. The question God asked Ezekiel He has never once let me answer with statistics. He asks it of every pastor standing in a valley with a spreadsheet and a roof that will not last the winter. Can these bones live. The only faithful answer is the prophet's answer, the answer that refuses both the lie of optimism and the lie of despair. O Lord God, you know. Then we open our mouths, and we speak the word we did not write, and we wait for a wind that has raised the dead before.

The church is not yours to save. It never was.

### Works Cited

Newbigin, Lesslie. 1986. Foolishness to the Greeks: The Gospel and Western Culture. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Newbigin, Lesslie. 1989. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1993. The Contemplative Pastor: Returning to the Art of Spiritual Direction. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge: Harvard University Press.

title: Why Churches Close, and What Comes Next
excerpt: A church does not die when it locks the door but years earlier, the day it stopped believing it had anything the lost could not get elsewhere.
body:
I have stood in a sanctuary the week before it closed. The pews were still there, the hymnals still in the racks, the offering plates stacked on a table in the narthex like dishes after the last guest has gone. An older woman walked me through it, naming the rooms, the nursery where her children had been dedicated, the kitchen where they had served funeral luncheons for sixty years. She was not crying. She had cried years earlier, she told me, when she first understood it was over, long before anyone said it aloud. That is the thing about a church closing. By the time the door is locked, the death is old news. The body was cooling for a decade while everyone kept setting the table.

We ask the wrong question when a church closes. We ask what went wrong at the end, as if the cause were proximate, a bad pastor, a building too big, a neighborhood that changed. Those are symptoms, and treating symptoms as causes is how we keep getting blindsided. The real question is harder and older. Why does a community that began with people willing to die for a crucified man end as a few faithful souls maintaining a building out of loyalty to the dead. The answer is rarely a scandal. The answer is usually a slow, respectable forgetting, a forgetting so gradual that no one in it could name the day it became fatal.

The data is not in dispute, and I will only use what is solid. Lifeway Research, working with denominational figures, estimated that roughly forty-five hundred Protestant churches closed in the United States in 2019 while about three thousand opened, a net loss in a single year (Earls 2021). Pew Research has tracked the share of Americans who claim no religion climbing from sixteen percent in 2007 to roughly twenty-eight percent by the early 2020s, the so-called nones now rivaling any single Christian tradition in size (Pew Research Center 2024). These are real numbers and they describe a real bleeding. But numbers explain that churches are closing. They do not explain why. For that you have to go further back than any chart reaches.

The strongest argument against pastoral hand-wringing deserves a fair hearing, because it is mostly right. The secularization theorists said this was coming and named the mechanism. Peter Berger argued for years that modernity dissolves the plausibility of belief, that when a society offers a thousand competing accounts of reality, no single sacred canopy can hold, and faith that once felt like the air becomes a choice that feels increasingly strange (Berger 1967, 127). On this account, churches close not because pastors failed but because the social conditions that made belief easy simply evaporated, and no amount of faithfulness could have held back a tide that size. There is real truth here, and pastors who pretend otherwise are lying to themselves. We did not cause the secular age and we cannot reverse it by trying harder. But Berger himself, to his great credit, recanted the strongest form of his own theory near the end of his life, conceding that the world had not become less religious, only that the West had, and that the simple story of inevitable decline did not survive contact with the actual planet (Berger 1999, 2). So the steel-manned version is not that secularization is a law of history. It is that secularization removed the social scaffolding that propped up nominal faith. And that distinction is the whole of the matter, because what secularization actually did was expose churches that had been living on scaffolding instead of on Christ.

Here is the text I cannot put down when I think about closed churches. To the church in Sardis, the risen Christ dictates a sentence that should make every pastor cold. I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead (Revelation 3:1 ESV). Sardis was a real congregation in a wealthy city, a church with a name, a brand, a standing. From the street it looked alive. The reputation was intact. And the verdict from the only One whose verdict counts was that the reputation had outlived the reality. That is how churches close. Not in a moment of dramatic apostasy but in a long stretch where the name stays alive after the life has left, where the reputation does the breathing the Spirit used to do. The closed church I walked through still had its name on the sign the week it died. Sardis always does.

Trace the root and the years line up. The slow death of the Western church did not begin with the nineties or the sixties. Mark Noll located a deeper failure in the way American Christianity, especially evangelicalism, had spent a century neglecting the life of the mind, building a faith long on feeling and short on the intellectual seriousness that could survive a hostile age (Noll 1994, 3). A church that cannot think cannot answer its children's questions, and a church that cannot answer its children loses them one confirmation class at a time, and the loss does not show on the attendance sheet for twenty years because the grandparents keep coming. By the time the demographics turn, the cause is three generations upstream. We buried our seriousness in 1925 and locked the door in 2019 and called it a building problem.

Now the reversal, because the gospel does not end at the autopsy. The most important fact about a closed church is the one we never say at the funeral. The closing of a congregation is not the closing of the kingdom. We grieve the building because we confused the building with the body, and we confused the body with the kingdom, and Christ never made either mistake. He told a parable about a seed that has to fall into the ground and die before it can bear any fruit at all (John 12:24 ESV). The seed that refuses to die stays a single seed, intact, respectable, alone, exactly like a church guarding its survival until survival is all it has left to worship. The churches that close having spent themselves on the lost are not the tragedy. The tragedy is the churches that close having spent themselves on staying open.

This is where the law has to land before any comfort comes. The law says that some churches close because of sin we would rather call circumstance. We loved our preferences more than our neighbors. We made the music, the carpet, the order of service into hills we defended while the mission field outside the doors went unvisited. I have sat in those meetings. I have watched a congregation spend its last energy fighting over a thing that would not matter in heaven, and I have stayed quiet when I should have named it, which makes me part of it. The law does not let me stand outside this. Andrew Root has written that the secular age has not only thinned belief but accelerated everything, leaving churches frantically busy and spiritually exhausted, mistaking activity for life (Root 2019, 6). The law says our busyness was not faithfulness. It was the death rattle of a body that no longer trusted the Spirit to do the breathing.

And then grace, which is the only word that makes a closed church bearable. The God we serve has never needed the institution to survive in order to keep His promise. He buried His own Son and the burial was not the end of the story but the hinge of it. So what comes next, after a church closes, is what has always come next when something falls into the ground in faith. The seed that died in one congregation rises in the people it formed, the children it baptized who carry the word into rooms that building never reached, the resources released to plant where the soil is ready. I have seen a closed church give its building to a young congregation that filled it within two years. The name on the sign changed. The kingdom did not lose a square foot.

Not every church should be saved. Some should be buried with honor, hands open, the way you bury a saint who finished the race. The sin is not in dying. The sin is in pretending to live while refusing to either repent or rest. Sardis could have woken up. The text begged her to. Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die (Revelation 3:2 ESV). Some did. Some did not. The door locks either way. The kingdom does not.

The building was never the church. We knew that. We forgot it slowly, the way men forget the thing they cannot afford to remember.

### Works Cited

Berger, Peter L. 1967. The Sacred Canopy: Elements of a Sociological Theory of Religion. Garden City: Doubleday.

Berger, Peter L. 1999. The Desecularization of the World: Resurgent Religion and World Politics. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Earls, Aaron. 2021. Protestant Church Closures Outpace Openings in U.S. Nashville: Lifeway Research.

Noll, Mark A. 1994. The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Pew Research Center. 2024. Religious Terrain Study. Washington: Pew Research Center.

Root, Andrew. 2019. The Pastor in a Secular Age: Ministry to People Who No Longer Need a God. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic.

title: Why Gen Z Is Coming Back to Church
excerpt: The young are not returning to be comforted but to be told the truth, and the church that flatters them will lose them again.
body:
A nineteen-year-old asked to meet me at a coffee shop last spring. He had been raised on nothing, no church, no catechism, a household where religion was treated the way you treat an old superstition, with a shrug. And he had spent two years reading, watching, arguing online, and now he sat across from me and said he thought it might all be true, the cross, the resurrection, the whole improbable claim, and he wanted to know if I believed it or just performed it. He was not looking for a welcome. He had welcomes everywhere. He was looking for someone who would not lie to him. I recognized him immediately, because I was him. I came to faith from atheism, and no one ever won me with comfort.

So I want to be careful with the headline, because the truth underneath it is more interesting than the headline. Something is stirring among the young, and the question is not whether it is happening but what it actually is and whether the church is about to misread it the way we misread every revival, by congratulating ourselves and then smothering the fire with our own enthusiasm. The real question is not how to get Gen Z back. The real question is what they are actually hungry for, because if we answer the wrong hunger we will fill the building for a season and empty it for a generation.

The data is genuinely mixed, and I will not pretend it says more than it does. The long decline of religious affiliation among the young is real and well documented, and Pew Research has shown the nones concentrated heavily in the youngest adults (Pew Research Center 2024). But more recent reporting complicates the simple story of collapse. The Bible Society in Britain, in its 2025 Quiet Revival study with YouGov, found church attendance among eighteen to twenty-four year olds rising sharply over six years, with young men in particular returning at rates no one predicted (Bible Society 2025). In the United States, some surveys have suggested the decades-long slide in Christian affiliation has at least leveled, with Pew noting the share of Christians holding roughly steady after years of falling (Pew Research Center 2024). I will not build a cathedral on a single survey. But the man across the coffee table was not a statistic, and he was not alone, and pastors are seeing his face more often than the decline narrative predicted.

Now the strongest objection, and it is a serious one. A skeptic, or a cautious pastor, will say this is not a return to Christ at all but a return to belonging, that a lonely, anxious generation raised by screens is reaching for any community that will hold them, and that the church is simply the warmest building still standing. There is real force here. Charles Taylor described the modern self as buffered, sealed off from transcendence, but also haunted by what that sealing cost, restless inside its own immanence (Taylor 2007, 38). On this reading the young are not finding God. They are fleeing loneliness, and the church is a convenient refuge that a better-funded secular alternative could replace tomorrow. I take this seriously because it is partly true. Some of what looks like revival is just isolation looking for a room. But here is where the objection breaks. If belonging were all they wanted, they would choose belonging that costs nothing. They are not. The young man at the coffee shop was not drawn to the church that asked the least of him. He was drawn to the one that asked him to die and rise, that told him his life was not his own. You do not explain that by loneliness. Loneliness wants comfort. He wanted the truth even if it cost him everything, and that is a different hunger entirely.

The text that holds this is Augustine's, though he is quoting his own heart back to God. You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you (Augustine 2008, 3). Augustine wrote that in the fourth century about his own youth, a brilliant, sensual, exhausted young man who had tried philosophy, ambition, sex, and prestige, and found every one of them a door that opened onto another empty room. He is the original case study for what is happening now. Not a man argued into faith by evidence alone, but a man worn out by the failure of every immanent thing to hold the weight he kept placing on it. Gen Z has been handed the most complete buffet of immanent satisfactions in human history, every pleasure and distraction available on a device in their pocket, and a measurable share of them have eaten the whole buffet by twenty and found themselves still hungry. The restlessness Augustine named is not a bug in the secular age. It is the secular age failing to deliver on its only promise.

Trace the root and the irony sharpens. The generation that is stirring was raised by the most thoroughly secular parenting in Western history, the children of the children of the sixties, formed by a culture that told them the self was sovereign and meaning was self-authored and no story was truer than any other. And it did not make them free. It made them anxious. The mental health data on this generation is grim and not in dispute, and a self handed total authorship of its own meaning turns out to be a self crushed under a weight it was never built to carry. Newbigin saw the shape of this coming, that a culture which severs fact from value and locks faith out of the realm of public truth leaves its young with private feelings and no public ground to stand on (Newbigin 1989, 16). We built them a world with no floor and called it liberation. Some of them have stopped falling long enough to ask whether there was ever a floor.

Here is the reversal the church most needs to hear, and it cuts against our instinct. The young are not coming back because we became more like them. They are coming back, where they are coming back, because the world became exactly like them and it was unbearable. The seeker-sensitive instinct of the last forty years was to strip the church of everything strange, to make the service feel like the culture so the culture would feel at home. And the culture did feel at home, which is precisely the problem, because a generation drowning in the culture does not want one more building that feels like it. They want the smell of something older than their anxiety. Reverence. Mystery. A word spoken with authority by someone who did not invent it. Eugene Peterson warned us for decades that the pastor's job was never to entertain but to pay attention to the holy and refuse the role of religious salesman (Peterson 1993, 18). The churches reaching the young are, strikingly, often the ones that never apologized for being churches.

And here the law has to come before the grace, or we will flatter them to death. The law says this generation has been lied to, and some of us did the lying. We told them the gospel was mainly therapeutic, a tool for their flourishing, Christ as life coach, and they tried it and found it thin, because a gospel that exists to serve the self cannot save the self from itself. The hard word the young are actually responding to is the word we have been too cowardly to preach. That they are sinners, that the cross was necessary and not merely nice, that following Christ will cost them the very autonomy their whole culture told them to defend. The law indicts me here. I have softened the cross to keep a room comfortable. I have preached the resurrection and skipped the death it required. And the young can smell that evasion from across the sanctuary. They have been marketed to their entire lives, and they recognize a sales pitch faster than any generation before them.

Which is why the grace, when it comes clean, lands so hard on them. A generation exhausted by performing, by curating, by the relentless labor of authoring its own worth, hears that righteousness is a gift it cannot earn and weeps. The young man at the coffee shop did not come to faith because I made it easy. He came because I told him the truth, that he could not save himself, that Christ already had, and that the only thing left for him to do was to stop running and receive it. He was baptized in the fall. He still asks hard questions. I hope he never stops.

The church that wins this generation by flattering it will lose it again within a decade, because flattery is exactly what they are fleeing. The church that tells them the truth, the whole weight of it, law and cross and grave and empty tomb, will find them more ready to hear it than we have any right to expect. They have tried the world we built for them. They are restless. We know what that means. We were restless too.

Do not give them comfort. Give them Christ.

### Works Cited

Augustine. 2008. Confessions. Translated by Henry Chadwick. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Bible Society. 2025. The Quiet Revival. London: Bible Society and YouGov.

Newbigin, Lesslie. 1989. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Peterson, Eugene H. 1993. The Contemplative Pastor: Returning to the Art of Spiritual Direction. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Pew Research Center. 2024. Religious Terrain Study. Washington: Pew Research Center.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge: Harvard University Press.

title: Replanting: When a Church Has to Start Over
excerpt: Replanting asks a congregation to do the one thing flesh resists most, to lay down its own life so that something it will not control can rise in its place.
body:
The vote was twenty-three to nine. Twenty-three older members of a congregation that had run six hundred strong in 1978 agreed to dissolve as they were and hand their building, their name, their endowment, and their Sunday morning to a replant they would not lead and could barely recognize. I was in the room as an outside voice, and I watched a woman in her eighties raise her hand for yes with tears running down her face. Afterward I asked her how she could vote to end the church she had given her life to. She said it was the only way to keep it from ending. Then she said something I have not been able to shake. We are not voting to die. We are voting to be buried, which is different, because you only bury what you expect to see again.

Replanting is the hardest word in this whole vocabulary, harder than revitalization, because revitalization still lets a church believe it is fundamentally the same body getting healthier. Replanting does not. Replanting says this body, as it is, cannot continue, and that the most faithful thing it can do is hand its life to a new work that will keep very little of what it was. The real question in a replant is not strategic. It is spiritual to the bone. Can a congregation love Christ and His mission more than it loves its own continuation. Almost everything else is logistics. That one question is the whole war.

Let me steel-man the people who say no, because they are not villains and the easy caricature of them is a lie. The members who resist a replant are usually accused of selfishness, of clinging to the carpet and the casseroles. But the strongest version of their position is not selfish at all. They will say that a church is not an interchangeable franchise, that it is a particular people with a particular history, that the saints buried in its memory and the prayers prayed in its walls are not disposable, and that to wipe it all away and call the result the same church is a kind of forgery. There is real theological weight here. The communion of saints is not a brand to be relaunched. Tim Keller, who spent his career thinking about how churches start and renew, warned against treating congregations as mere delivery systems for programs, insisting that a church is a body with a history and a culture that cannot be engineered from a manual (Keller 2012, 19). So the honest version of the objection is this. Replanting risks treating a living tradition as scrap. And the answer to that objection is not to deny it but to go through it, because Scripture has a category for a death that honors what died precisely by refusing to embalm it.

The spine here is the same hard saying of Jesus that haunts every page of this subject. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24 ESV). Notice what the seed keeps and what it loses. It does not keep its shape. The husk is destroyed, dissolved in the dark, unrecognizable. But the seed keeps its life, its very specific genetic identity, and what rises is not a different plant but the same life in a form the seed could never have produced by staying intact. This is the exact answer to the objection. Replanting done faithfully is not the erasure of a tradition. It is the burial of a husk so that the life inside it can rise. The woman in her eighties understood the verse better than the consultants. You only bury what you expect to see again.

The history of this is older and more Protestant than we admit. We talk about replanting as a new movement of the last fifteen years, and the practical models are recent, but the underlying conviction runs back to the Reformation itself, which was at bottom a massive replant. The reformers did not believe they were inventing a new church. They believed they were recovering a buried one, that the institution had so encrusted the gospel that the only faithful move was to tear down structures and start the visible church again on the recovered foundation. Mark Noll has shown how the renewal movements that shaped Protestant vitality across the centuries came again and again through disruption rather than maintenance, through people willing to lose the existing form to recover the buried center (Noll 1992, 4). Replanting is not a betrayal of the inherited church. It is the inherited church doing the very thing it was born doing.

Now the reversal, and it is the one that converts a strategy into a death worth dying. We assume the replant is for the sake of the new people, the unreached neighborhood, the young families who will fill the rebuilt sanctuary. That is true but it is not the deepest truth. The replant is also, and maybe first, for the sake of the people voting yes. Because the act of laying down your own church for a future you will not control is itself the most Christlike thing many of those saints will ever do, and it forms them in the image of their Lord more than another decade of survival ever could. I have watched older believers come spiritually alive in the very act of agreeing to their congregation's death, freed at last from the exhausting work of keeping a dying thing propped up, released into the joy of pure gift. The replant did not just serve the new. It saved the old from the slow corrosion of self-preservation. Eugene Peterson said the pastoral task is to keep insisting that the most important things are the things we cannot make happen, only receive (Peterson 1987, 6). The yes vote is exactly that, a refusal to make survival happen, an opening of the hands.

The law has to be preached here without flinching, and it cuts the leader first. The law says that much of our resistance to replanting is idolatry wearing the mask of faithfulness. We say we are protecting the legacy, and sometimes we are protecting our own importance, our own grief, our own fear of admitting that what we built could not last. I have felt this in myself. I have wanted a thing I led to outlive me more than I have wanted Christ to be honored in its ending, and that wanting is not love, it is the same self-preservation the gospel came to kill. The law strips the noble language off the fear and shows it for what it is. A church that will not die for the mission has already started worshiping itself, and the slow death that follows is not tragedy. It is judgment.

And then grace, which is the only thing that makes the burial bearable. The grace is that the God who asks the seed to fall into the earth is the same God who went into the earth first. Christ did not ask of any congregation a death He had not already died, alone, in the dark, with no guarantee visible to flesh that anything would rise. And because He rose, the burial of a faithful church is not a leap into nothing. It is a leap into the pattern of the only One who has ever come back from where He went. The endowment becomes seed. The building becomes soil. The saints who voted yes become, in their final ministry, the very wheat their Lord described, and what rises in that place will carry their life in a form they could not have imagined and will, I believe, one day recognize.

Not every church should be replanted. Some have the health to be revitalized and should be. Some are too far gone for either and should be buried with honor and no pretense of resurrection in this age. Discernment is the whole art, and it cannot be reduced to a flowchart. But where a replant is the faithful road, the church that takes it is not surrendering. It is doing the most ancient Christian thing there is. It is following its Lord into the ground, in the stubborn confidence that the ground is not the end of the story but the one place the story has always begun.

You only bury what you expect to see again. The saints knew that before the consultants did.

### Works Cited

Keller, Timothy. 2012. Center Church: Doing Balanced, Gospel-Centered Ministry in Your City. Grand Rapids: Zondervan.

title: Leading a Church When Trust Is Gone
excerpt: Trust cannot be restored by competence or charisma but only by the slow, costly work of a leader who tells the truth when the truth indicts him.
body:
I followed a man who had lied to the congregation for years. Not about money, which would have been simpler, but about who he was, a pattern of deception that came apart all at once and left a church of good people unable to believe anything said from the pulpit, including the things that were true. I arrived eight months after he left. The wound was not in the budget. It was in the eyes. People listened to me preach with their arms folded, not because they disliked me but because the last man had stood in the same spot and sounded sincere, and look what that was worth. You cannot lead people who have learned that listening is dangerous. And they had learned it from a master.

The instinct in that situation is to rebuild trust by being trustworthy, by being competent and consistent and clearly not the last guy, and that instinct is not wrong but it is not nearly enough. The real question when trust is gone is not how the leader proves himself. The real question is whether the leader understands that broken trust is not primarily a problem to be solved but a wound to be grieved, and that the people are not being difficult, they are being faithful to an injury they did not ask for. A pastor who treats lost trust as an obstacle to his leadership has already revealed that he does not understand it. The lost trust is not in his way. It is the thing he is there to serve.

Here is the strongest case against my whole approach, and it comes from sharp people who have watched too many churches paper over real harm. They will say that talk of rebuilding trust is often a tool of institutional self-protection, that when leaders call for unity and healing they usually mean be quiet and let us move on, and that the demand for renewed trust frequently falls hardest on the very people who were hurt, asking the wounded to extend something to the institution that wounded them. This is not cynicism. It is observation, and it is frequently correct. The history of the church's handling of abuse and deception is a history of premature calls for reconciliation that served the powerful and silenced the harmed. I have to grant this in full, because to wave it away would be to commit the exact sin it names. So the honest version of the objection is this. Trust language is often a weapon against the wounded. And the only answer that is not itself a dodge is to insist that real trust can never be rebuilt by asking the hurt to pretend. It can only be rebuilt by leaders willing to stand inside the indictment rather than above it.

The text I carry into these churches is the most uncomfortable restoration scene in the New Testament. Peter had denied Christ three times, publicly, by a fire, when it cost something to be loyal. And the risen Jesus does not restore him with a warm word and a clean slate. By a charcoal fire, the same kind of fire Peter stood at when he lied, Jesus asks him three times, once for each denial, do you love me (John 21:15 ESV). It is not gentle. The text says Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time (John 21:17 ESV). Jesus rebuilds trust by walking Peter straight back into the smell of his own failure and refusing to let him skip past it. This is the pattern, and it is the opposite of how we usually do it. We rebuild trust by changing the subject. Christ rebuilds it by returning to the wound, naming it fully, and only then speaking the future. Feed my sheep. The commission comes after the fire, never instead of it.

The history of this in the church is long and not flattering, and naming it is part of the repair. The crises of trust that have hollowed out congregations across the last several decades, the financial scandals, the abuse coverups, the celebrity pastors whose private lives contradicted every public word, did not erode trust by accident. They eroded it through a consistent institutional reflex to protect the name over the truth, exactly the Sardis reflex, reputation kept alive after integrity had died. Sociologists of religion have noted that institutional trust in nearly every Western institution, the church among them, has fallen steadily since the nineteen seventies, and the church accelerated its own fall every time it chose the cover story over confession (Berger 1999, 11). We were not merely victims of a cynical age. We taught a watching world to distrust us, one cover-up at a time, and the young especially have learned the lesson well.

Now the reversal, the thing that took me three years in that wounded church to learn. The leader cannot rebuild trust by being trusted. He rebuilds it by being trustworthy in a way that does not depend on whether anyone trusts him yet, and that means his faithfulness has to be aimed past the congregation's approval entirely. The moment I needed their trust in order to lead, I made my leadership a transaction, and they could smell the need, and the need is exactly what the last man had. He needed their belief and so he managed his image to secure it. The only way I could be different was to stop needing their trust and start simply telling the truth, including the truths that cost me, including the times I was wrong in front of them, with no anxious eye on whether it was working. Trust, it turns out, is never built by the man who is trying to build it. It is the slow accidental fruit of a man who has stopped trying and started confessing. Eugene Peterson said that the pastor's integrity is in the unseen disciplines, the angles no congregation watches, and that a ministry built for the visible approval rots at the unseen root (Peterson 1987, 2).

So the law comes, and it comes for the leader before it comes for the people who broke trust. The law says that a pastor inheriting a wounded church will be tempted to use the wound, to position himself as the trustworthy rescuer against the villain who left, and that this self-positioning is its own quiet lie. I have done it. I have let a congregation's relief at my arrival become a thing I enjoyed too much, have let myself be the hero of a story whose real hero is Christ and whose real victims deserved more lament than I gave them. The law indicts the rescuer fantasy. It says that the man who rebuilds trust by being the not-villain is still making the church about himself, just in a more flattering pose. I cannot stand outside this. I am exactly the kind of leader who would rather be admired for honesty than actually pay its cost.

And then grace, which is the only ground a wounded church can finally stand on. The grace is that the trust the congregation most needs to recover is not trust in their leaders, who will fail them again because all leaders are men, but trust in the Christ who restored Peter at the fire and did not flinch from the wound. A church whose trust in its pastors has been destroyed has, painfully, been freed from an idol it should never have had. It was never safe to put ultimate trust in a man. The collapse of that trust, brutal as it is, can become the doorway to a deeper and unbreakable trust in the only One who has never once managed His image, who told the truth about us at the cost of His life, and who returns to our fires not to shame us but to commission us. Feed my sheep is spoken to a man who failed and was not pretended past it. That is the only kind of leader a broken church can follow. One who knows the fire.

Trust does not come back when the leader proves he is worthy. It comes back, slowly, when the leader stops needing it and starts telling the truth, especially the truth that costs him. There is no shortcut. There was none for Peter. There is none for me.

The fire is where it starts. We would rather it started anywhere else.
